title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing — September 1, 2026 (Catch-Up Cycle: A 2023 Source Passed as 2026, and a Harm Below the Filing Floor)
headline: A 2026 UN finding cited for Chile turned out to be dated 2023 — caught before it was published.
summary:
Chile's steepest score change tonight came with a warning built into it. A search summary handed the benchmark what looked like a fresh 2026 UN finding on Chile's migration crackdown. It even included specific numbers on how long migrants could be detained. When the underlying pages were opened directly, they were dated 2023, and the real detention figures were different. All of it was thrown out before it could be used. Chile's score still falls 20 points, from 62.5 to 42.5 of 100, crossing from the Established band into the Functional band. The fall rests on a real migrant-registration freeze, deportation flights, and a package of emergency-powers amendments that survived the check. But the benchmark's own rule for confirming a band change this way was not met on what remained, so the finding is logged, not confirmed.

A second finding tonight is not about a wrong number. It is about a real one the benchmark cannot record. Ethiopia's federal military struck targets across the Tigray region through August, including a school in a populated village. That deterioration is real and measured at 2.8 points. But Ethiopia's published score, 4.7 of 100, was already only 4.7 points above zero. The benchmark only logs a change of 5 points or more. Four other entities — Sudan, Israel, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Haiti — hit the same wall tonight. Each sits so close to the floor that a genuine decline has less room to move than the benchmark's own rule requires to record one.

Three more findings were filed. Regions Financial falls 38.4 points after a $191 million federal order for overdraft fees. The bank was fined for the same conduct once already, in 2015. Most of the fall reflects a placeholder score the bank had never been individually reviewed on, not new misconduct. Kenya falls 5.9 points on a third protest-policing incident in three cycles. It is a threshold the benchmark set for itself in writing, before the incident happened. Starbucks falls 5.3 points on an unresolved five-year contract dispute. The labor union's boycott itself was excluded, because a campaign against a company is not the company's own conduct.

None of the four findings were applied to the published rankings tonight. Two other reviews turned into corrections instead of scores. McKesson's headline breach — 284 million patient records, by the attacker's own count — turned out to be a row count, not a person count. The attacker admitted it did not know how many people were affected, and McKesson's score barely moved. And a reported killing in Peru resurfaced through news wires that had not caught up to its own retraction from a week earlier. The benchmark caught the same false story a second time before it could be published again.

pipeline.rosterNote: The roster held at 1,331 entities this cycle. A gap-fill run covered the six days left uncovered after the 2026-08-26 cycle closed, from 27 August through 1 September.
pipeline.queueHandling: Twenty organizations were checked across the six-day catch-up window. Four findings were filed and sixteen scores were confirmed unchanged. None of the four findings were applied to the published rankings. Two findings cross a published band; the other two are magnitude-only findings within their current band. Three further band crossings were measured in the same rotation batch but were not filed, because they reflect an unreviewed placeholder score shared across four entities rather than new conduct.

topSignals.title: Chile's Score Falls 20 Points — Part of the Evidence Behind It Was Three Years Old, and the Benchmark Caught It
topSignals.whyItMatters: A source that looked like a fresh 2026 UN finding on Chile turned out to date from 2023. Real 2026 conduct still drives the fall, but the band crossing itself is not yet proven.
topSignals.description: A search summary for Chile appeared to surface a 2026 United Nations finding on migrant detention, complete with specific figures: detention extended from five days to sixty, renewable to a hundred eighty, plus a requirement that hospitals, schools and social security offices hand migrants' data to immigration authorities. On direct verification, the underlying Global Detention Project pages are dated June and December 2023, and the UN communication they quote is dated May 2023 — three years outside this cycle's window. The real 2023 detention figures are different again (forty-eight hours to seven days, not five days to sixty), and the healthcare-and-school data-sharing claim appears in neither page. All of it was excluded before it could be scored. What survived is real and dated inside the window: Chile's government suspended a decree that would have regularized roughly 182,000 already-registered migrants, launched deportation flights, and in August submitted eight constitutional amendments that would allow a public-safety emergency of up to two hundred forty days without congressional approval — which Human Rights Watch called "a dangerous power grab" that "puts the rights of all Chileans at risk." On that surviving evidence, Chile's score falls twenty points, from 62.5 to 42.5 of 100, crossing from the Established band into the Functional band. A crossing of that kind needs at least one high-authority source — a UN body, court or international organization — and none was found once the 2023 material was removed. The finding is filed as unproven rather than confirmed.

evidence.quote: This is a dangerous power grab that puts the rights of all Chileans at risk.
evidence.claim: Human Rights Watch characterized the Kast government's eight constitutional amendments as a power grab endangering rights.

evidence.quote: do not align or attempt to align with these human rights frameworks
evidence.claim: Human Rights Watch found the amendment package does not engage the international frameworks governing emergency rights derogations.

evidence.quote: We are not going to carry out a mass regularization like the one proposed under the Boric government.
evidence.claim: Chile's National Migration Service head confirmed suspension of the regularization decree covering about 182,000 registered migrants.

evidence.quote: The Kast government has already sent two bills to congress which would criminalise illegal entry, as well as limit immigrants' access to social security benefits.
evidence.claim: Legislation before Chile's Congress would remove a named population's access to social security.

topSignals.title: Ethiopia's Military Struck Its Own Region, Including a School — the Benchmark's Scale Has No Room Left to Record It
topSignals.whyItMatters: Ethiopia's own military conducted drone strikes across Tigray, hitting a school. The 2.8-point decline this produced could not be logged — the score had less room to fall than the benchmark's own rule requires.
topSignals.description: The Ethiopian National Defence Force has conducted drone strikes across the Tigray region since mid-August, according to Critical Threats — the first sustained military confrontation there since the 2022 peace deal. One strike, on 10 August, hit an out-of-session school in the village of Merewa where fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front were reportedly sheltering. Whether civilians were killed is disputed between AFP and the BBC, and the benchmark does not score the disputed casualty count in either direction — it scores the decision to strike a school in a populated village. A search summary earlier this cycle had credited Amnesty International with describing these drone strikes. Amnesty's article does not mention drone strikes at all, and is dated 3 August, twenty-four days before the evidence window opened; its forced-conscription findings are attributed by Amnesty to Tigrayan regional authorities, not the federal government. The correction moved the conduct finding off Amnesty and onto Critical Threats, where the evidence actually is. The assessed decline is 2.8 points, from a published 4.7 to 1.9 of 100. Ethiopia's published score was already only 4.7 points above zero, and the benchmark only records a change of 5 points or more. A real, sourced deterioration inside a country's own military conduct could not be logged. Four other entities — Sudan, Israel, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Haiti — sit in the same position tonight, each with less room to fall than the benchmark's own filing rule requires.

evidence.quote: an out-of-session school where TPLF fighters were sheltering
evidence.claim: The Ethiopian National Defence Force struck a school building in the village of Merewa during a sustained drone-strike campaign across Tigray.

evidence.quote: restore access for independent media and human rights monitors
evidence.claim: Amnesty International called on Ethiopia's federal government to restore access for independent monitors and media to Tigray.

topSignals.title: Regions Financial Falls 38 Points — Most of That Is a Placeholder Score Finally Reviewed, Not New Misconduct
topSignals.whyItMatters: A federal order fined Regions Financial $191 million for overdraft fees, repeating a 2015 violation. But most of its 38-point fall corrects a score the bank had never actually been reviewed on.
topSignals.description: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered Regions Bank to pay $191 million — $141 million in consumer refunds and a $50 million penalty — for charging overdraft fees on transactions after telling customers they had sufficient funds. It is a repeat: the CFPB had already ordered Regions in 2015 to refund $49 million and pay a $7.5 million penalty for the same category of overdraft failure, seven years earlier. Regions' published score of 60.9 of 100 was never the product of an individual review. It was a placeholder shared, digit for digit, with three other Fortune 500 entities — Nationwide, Principal Financial and Raymond James Financial — all never assessed and all sitting at consecutive ranks 44 through 48. Those three, carrying no adverse evidence of their own, assess at 25.0, 25.6 and 26.9 once reviewed for the first time — that range is what an honest first look produces from absence of disclosure alone. Regions assesses at 22.5, two to four points lower, and that smaller gap is the real conduct component of tonight's finding. The other three were confirmed unchanged with no proposal filed, because a shared placeholder score is a calibration question, not a one-off conduct finding. Regions was filed anyway, because letting an Established-band label stand against a documented $141 million consumer-harm order would leave a label the record itself contradicts.

evidence.quote: CFPB Orders Regions Bank to Pay $191 Million for Illegal Surprise Overdraft Fees
evidence.claim: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau imposed a $191 million order on Regions Bank for illegal surprise overdraft fees.
The 2022 order describes the same category of overdraft-fee violation the CFPB had already penalized Regions for in 2015.

evidence.quote: CFPB fines Regions $191M on overdraft practices
evidence.claim: Independent trade-press corroboration of the $191 million CFPB action against Regions Bank.

topSignals.title: Kenya Falls 5.9 Points on a Third Protest-Policing Incident — a Rule the Benchmark Set for Itself in Advance
topSignals.whyItMatters: Kenyan police tear-gassed protesting traders on 28 August — the third documented protest-policing incident in three cycles, triggering a downgrade rule the benchmark wrote before this incident happened.
topSignals.description: Kenyan police fired tear gas at small-scale traders protesting an import-duty increase in central Nairobi on 28 August 2026, closing hundreds of businesses. It is the third documented protest-policing incident across three consecutive review cycles: abductions and brutality during a 25 June protest, now under investigation by Kenya's Independent Policing Oversight Authority; six activists arrested outside police headquarters on 17 August while demanding the police chief's resignation; and the 28 August tear-gassing. The benchmark's own prior review, on 18 August, committed in writing to escalate to a formal finding if a third incident landed — it has landed. IPOA has been investigating protest-policing brutality since June, and protest policing continued unchanged through two further incidents in the meantime, which is scored as a failure to correct course on evidence Kenya's own oversight body was already examining. Counted in Kenya's favor: IPOA itself is a funded, active oversight body, and the Kenya Revenue Authority publicly defended and explained the contested customs measure. The triggering 28 August incident rests on a single news source, which reports no injury or arrest count; the finding's real weight comes from the three-incident pattern, independently corroborated across four sources.

evidence.quote: fired tear gas at small-scale traders who are protesting against a hike in import duties
evidence.claim: Kenyan police dispersed a protest by small traders in central Nairobi with tear gas on 28 August 2026.

evidence.quote: IPOA probes June 25 protest abductions, police brutality
evidence.claim: Kenya's own Independent Policing Oversight Authority opened an investigation into a June protest-policing incident, the first of the three now on record.

topSignals.title: Starbucks Falls 5.3 Points on an Unresolved Contract Dispute — a Union Boycott Was Excluded Entirely
topSignals.whyItMatters: Starbucks and its unionized baristas remain without a first contract after nearly five years. A boycott campaign against the company was not scored, because it is not the company's own conduct.
topSignals.description: Starbucks Workers United has not concluded a first contract with a bargaining unit that organized in late 2021 — approaching five years of negotiation. The union announced a boycott on 25 August, joined by the AFL-CIO and a vote from the Chicago Teachers Union. None of that is scored: a boycott, a labor federation's endorsement and another union's vote are actions taken by other organizations, not by Starbucks itself. Union-asserted counts of unfair-labor-practice violations — reported variously as 550, more than 700, and more than 400 — come from a party to the dispute, contradict each other by more than 150, and could not be verified against a primary National Labor Relations Board record, so none of them was used. What remains, once third-party conduct is excluded, is thinner: another month without a contract, and a company statement restating its bargaining position rather than acknowledging the delay. Counted in Starbucks' favor: a 2026 federal appeals court decision vacated an earlier unfair-labor-practice ruling against the company, and Starbucks continues to provide part-time health coverage and tuition support. The finding is filed on the magnitude of the movement, not as a confident downgrade — the evidence for a 5.3-point fall is real but thin, and a reasonable reading of the same facts could land on a smaller number.

evidence.quote: As we have always been, we're committed to engaging in productive bargaining.
evidence.claim: Starbucks restated its bargaining position in response to the boycott announcement rather than acknowledging the five-year delay.

evidence.quote: been trying to get a contract with the coffee giant since late 2021
evidence.claim: The Starbucks bargaining unit organized in late 2021 and has not reached a first contract.

topSignals.title: McKesson's Headline Breach Figure Doesn't Hold Up — the Company's Score Barely Moves
topSignals.whyItMatters: A hacking group claimed 284 million patient records stolen from McKesson. The group's own clarification says the number counts database rows, not people, and McKesson confirmed no patient count.
topSignals.description: The extortion group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen roughly 284 million patient data records from McKesson, the healthcare distributor. The figure does not hold up under verification. The group itself later clarified the number is "a raw count of approximately 284 million data records, or lines, rather than a count of unique individuals," and told reporters it was "unsure of how many individuals are ultimately affected." McKesson has confirmed no patient count of its own. No patient figure is used anywhere in this review. What is verified: McKesson discovered the intrusion on 25 August and filed publicly with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on 28 August — three days, faster than the law required, since the filing was made under a voluntary disclosure rule rather than the mandatory one for material incidents. In the same filing, McKesson stated it "has not determined that the incident is material." The filing says nothing about notifying the people whose records were affected; it directs stakeholders to the company's website. Fast, voluntary disclosure to investors and no evidenced outreach to patients roughly offset each other, and McKesson's score moves down just 0.7 points, from 31.3 to 30.6 of 100, remaining in the Developing band.

evidence.quote: a raw count of approximately 284 million data records, or lines, rather than a count of unique individuals
evidence.claim: The hacking group ShinyHunters itself clarified that its 284-million figure counts database rows, not people.

evidence.quote: unsure of how many individuals are ultimately affected
evidence.claim: The hackers who claimed the breach told reporters they did not know how many people were actually affected.

evidence.quote: On August 25, 2026, McKesson Corporation discovered a cybersecurity incident affecting its information systems.
evidence.claim: McKesson's own SEC filing confirms the discovery date, three days before its voluntary public disclosure.

topSignals.title: A Falsely Reported Killing in Peru Resurfaced Through Wire Pickups That Never Caught the Correction
topSignals.whyItMatters: A reported killing in Peru was already proven false a week earlier. It resurfaced this cycle through wire stories that had not caught up to the correction — the benchmark caught it a second time before publishing.
topSignals.description: On 26 August, the benchmark confirmed that a reported killing of Ashéninka leader Américo Pascual Tumisha in Peru's Ucayali region had not happened — the Indigenous federation that raised the original alert retracted it after a river patrol found him alive and safe. This cycle, the same false claim resurfaced, carried by wire pickups (Manila Times, Cambodianess) that had republished the original story on 26 August, the same day it was retracted, and had not caught up to the correction by the time this review ran. Direct verification against the retraction record confirmed the story remains false, and it was dropped again before it could be published a second time. Peru's score is unchanged from the 26 August review, at 36.2 of 100. A correctly dated news wire can still carry a story that has already been proven wrong — the second time in two consecutive cycles this exact failure pattern has been caught before publication.

topSignals.title: 3M Measured a Real Improvement Tonight — and Deliberately Did Not Publish It
topSignals.whyItMatters: 3M's conduct measured a real 5.3-point improvement this cycle, but the gain came from an old, already-completed change while the trigger for review was a new lawsuit — so it was not published as an upgrade.
topSignals.description: 3M was flagged this cycle over a lawsuit by the City of Hastings, Minnesota, alleging its Cottage Grove facility contaminated municipal drinking-water wells with PFOA chemicals. That allegation is unproven and is not scored as an established fact. What is scored is 3M's own conduct: the company promised in December 2022 to stop manufacturing PFAS chemicals by the end of 2025, and it completed that exit on schedule. Voluntarily ending a profitable product line on a self-imposed deadline is a genuine, costly course correction, and it measures a full 5.3 points higher than 3M's published score, from 20.3 to 25.6 of 100 — large enough to publish under the benchmark's own rules. It was not published. The positive conduct finished at the end of 2025, entirely outside the window that triggered this review, and 3M was flagged this cycle on new negative evidence, not on the completed PFAS exit. Publishing an upgrade in the same cycle a company is flagged for a new lawsuit, on conduct that predates the lawsuit by months, would be the wrong direction for the evidence rule to bend. This is the second consecutive cycle in which the benchmark has measured a real improvement and chosen not to publish it.

evidence.claim: 3M completed its self-imposed exit from PFAS chemical manufacturing on the schedule it set in 2022.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries — Attribution Discipline Holds in Both Directions
sectorAlerts.headline: Non-state conduct was consistently excluded from state scores across nine countries reviewed tonight, while state protective failures and responses were credited on both sides of the ledger.
observations: Chile (62.5 published, 42.5 proposed): a source that appeared to support a 2026 UN finding was dated 2023 and excluded; the remaining conduct still crosses a band.
Ethiopia (4.7 published, 1.9 confirmed): federal drone strikes hit a school in Tigray; the 2.8-point fall has no room left under the 5-point filing threshold.
Nigeria (18.0 published, 17.5 confirmed): the death toll was corrected to 1,142 from a scan figure of 963; non-state kidnapping conduct is not scored against the state.
India (15.6 published, 16.3 confirmed): two deaths in Kangpokpi were reattributed from the state to suspected militants after corroboration against four Indian outlets.

Haiti (4.7 published, 3.1 confirmed) and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (2.3 published, 3.1 confirmed): gang and rebel conduct held apart from state conduct in both cases; DRC's Ebola outbreak, the deadliest in its history, was incorporated.

methodologyNotes.name: A Correctly Dated Search Result Can Still Be Built From an Old Source
methodologyNotes.description: A search summary for Chile appeared to describe a fresh 2026 United Nations finding on migrant detention. On direct verification, the underlying source pages were dated 2023, three years outside the review window, and the specific figures in the summary did not match the real 2023 document. The material was excluded before it could be scored. This is the same failure pattern caught on Peru on 26 August: search synthesis can present old material as current, and only a direct check of the underlying source catches it.

methodologyNotes.name: A Score Near Zero Can Have Less Room to Fall Than the Rule Requires to Record It
methodologyNotes.description: Five entities this cycle — Sudan, Israel, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and Ethiopia — sit close enough to the bottom of the scale that a real, documented decline has less room to move than the benchmark's 5-point minimum for logging a change. Ethiopia's federal military striking a school in Tigray produced a real 2.8-point fall that could not be filed. A sub-floor severity marker, carried alongside the composite, has been proposed to let the record show a floor score is still getting worse.

methodologyNotes.name: A Placeholder Score and a Real Violation Can Sit on the Same Row
methodologyNotes.description: Four Fortune 500 entities shared an identical, never-individually-reviewed score of 60.9. Reviewing all four for the first time separated the placeholder effect (a 25.0-to-26.9 range with no adverse evidence) from real conduct: Regions Financial's federal $191 million overdraft-fee order, a repeat of a 2015 violation, added a further two to four points of documented harm on top of the placeholder gap.

methodologyNotes.name: An Improvement Measured on a Reactive Review Is Not Published as an Upgrade
methodologyNotes.description: 3M's own conduct measured a real 5.3-point improvement this cycle — a completed, on-schedule exit from PFAS chemical manufacturing. It was not published, because the positive conduct finished at the end of 2025, before the new lawsuit that triggered this cycle's review. Publishing an upgrade in the same cycle a company is newly flagged for unrelated allegations would credit the wrong evidence for the wrong reason. This is the second consecutive cycle this discipline has held.
